sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bacterial keratitis is a sight-threatening suppurative inflammation of the corneal stroma caused by bacterial invasion. It is characterized by the presence of a corneal epithelial defect with underlying stromal infiltration, often accompanied by significant anterior segment inflammation and pain. True emergencies require immediate culturing and intensive fortified antibiotic therapy.

branches: Gram (+) Cocci: S. aureus, S. epidermidis, S. pneumoniae
Gram (-) Rods: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CL wearers), Klebsiella, Proteus
Gram (-) Cocci: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Can penetrate intact epithelium)
Gram (+) Rods: Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Mycobacterium spp.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: 1. Epithelial Breakdown: Disruption of the protective barrier due to trauma or hypoxia.
2. Adhesion: Bacteria utilize fimbriae or pili to bind to damaged cells and collagen.
3. Invasion: Secretion of enzymes (proteases, elastases) to digest the stroma.
4. Host Response: Influx of PMNs and cytokine release leads to stromal necrosis and edema.

sections.title: Specific Organism 'Clues'
content: Pseudomonas: Rapid progression, greenish mucopurulent discharge, soupy melt.
S. pneumoniae: Serpiginous ulcer, often with significant hypopyon.
S. aureus: Round, well-demarcated white-grey infiltrate, relatively dry.
Moraxella: Oval ulcer, typically in the inferior cornea, seen in debilitated patients.

sections.title: Microbiological Investigation Protocol
content: 1. Topical Anesthesia (Proparacaine preferred over Tetracaine).
2. Scrape leading edge and base of the ulcer using a Kimura spatula or 25G needle.
3. Direct Inoculation onto Blood, Chocolate, and Sabouraud Agar.
4. Slide Preparation: Gram stain and Giemsa stain for immediate microscopy.
5. Culture Enrichment: Place sample in Thioglycolate broth.

branches: Fungal Keratitis: Feathery borders, satellite lesions
Acanthamoeba: Ring infiltrate, radial keratoneuritis, extreme pain
Viral (HSV): Geographic ulcer, decreased corneal sensation
Sterile Infiltrates: Peripheral, clear space from limbus, minimal pain
Marginal Keratitis: Associated with blepharitis, hypersensitivity to Staph

rows: Reduces ciliary spasm and prevents synechiae

sections.title: Landmark Study: The SCUT Trial
content: Trial: Steroids for Corneal Ulcers Trial (SCUT).
Finding 1: No overall difference in BCVA at 3 months with adjunctive steroids.
Finding 2: Significant benefit in VA for baseline severe ulcers (worst vision).
Finding 3: Nocardia ulcers worsened with steroids (contraindicated).
Conclusion: Steroids are safe after 48h of effective antibiotics, except in Nocardia.

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Concern
content: Descemetocele (Imminent Perforation)
Scleral extension of the infiltrate
Worsening pain despite treatment
Limbal involvement (potential for stem cell loss)
Rapid stromal melting within 24 hours

content.explanation: P: Pain (Severe), E: Epithelial defect (Size/Shape), D: Discharge (Purulent), A: Anterior chamber reaction (Hypopyon), L: Location (Central vs. Peripheral).

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: 1. Cyanoacrylate Tissue Glue: For small perforations (<2mm) or thinning.
2. Conjunctival Flap (Gundersen): For chronic non-healing ulcers.
3. Amniotic Membrane Transplant: Promotes epithelialization.
4. Therapeutic Keratoplasty: PKP or LKP for uncontrolled infection or perforation.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring/Leukoma: Results in irregular astigmatism and vision loss.
Endophthalmitis: Rare unless perforation occurs.
Secondary Glaucoma: Due to inflammatory debris in the trabecular meshwork.
Phthisis Bulbi: In severe, uncontrolled endophthalmitis cases.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Never use a 'Steroid-Antibiotic' combo (e.g., Tobradex) for an undiagnosed ulcer.
Document the size of the epithelial defect AND the infiltrate separately.
Fungal keratitis should be suspected if the ulcer doesn't respond to broad-spectrum antibiotics within 48-72h.
A 'culture-negative' ulcer may be caused by fastidious organisms or prior antibiotic use.
In contact lens wearers, always culture the lens case and solution if available.
